why: The wheels add 5 cm to the inner width, so a 10 cm chassis gives 15 cm overall. With the 1.0 cm sigma and the 2 cm offset of the opening, that still fits 20 cm. A 4 cm belly sits above the 2.5 cm hose, and the wheels already climb 3.05 cm on grass. Total height becomes 8 cm, still under the 9 cm sofa.

The HC-SR04 sonar ranges 2 m in any light, so the robot can stop well before each obstacle at full speed. That removes the 40 s of bump-and-back-off and brings the 8 m corridor well under 45 s. No sensor setting can fix this, because the bump switch has no range at all. Cost $2.50, 2 days.

Last time this was refused only on geometry: a 30 cm track on a 20 cm tub. Now the tub is 26 cm, matching a 26 cm track. That bridges about 0.45×26 ≈ 11.7 cm, more than the 9 cm trench. The 7 cm idler (track top at 8.5 cm) meets the 5.5 cm porch edge on the sloped run. The tub rides 4 cm above the track contact line, so the belly cannot ground on an edge the track is crossing. Sand pressure drops to a few hundred Pa, under 0.5 cm of sinkage. Tracks run one N20 per side through a 1.8 cm sprocket, so force per motor is about 1.67× the 3 cm wheel. The 2-cell Li-ion pack (7.4 V, inside the N20's 3–9 V) restores force and speed, giving about 0.7 m/s no-load. It also replaces the 8.16 Wh NiMH, which could not cover 5 km of tracked rolling resistance; I estimate about 7 J/m, so roughly 10 Wh, against about 16 Wh usable. I would buy rubber_track_kit $14, plus cell_18650 x2 $9 and bms_board $1.5 = $24.50. Lead time is 4 days. Printing the tub and track frames is about 230 machine min.
